title: 1987 decision to adopt binding international controls on ozone-depleting substances

decision_cutoff.date_or_period: September 1987 before adoption of the Montreal Protocol
decision_cutoff.definition: States deciding whether to adopt binding staged controls on production and consumption of chlorofluorocarbons and related ozone-depleting substances despite scientific uncertainty, industrial transition costs and unequal national capacities.

packets.masking_note: Names the ozone layer, CFCs, Vienna Convention and proposed Montreal Protocol.
Names/chemical labels removed; preserves global-atmospheric risk, scientific uncertainty, dispersed future harms, industrial costs and staged/reviewable international controls.

expected_constitutional_constraints: Scientific uncertainty does not require waiting for catastrophic certainty where a serious, plausible and potentially long-lived global harm pathway is supported by evidence.
Precaution must remain evidence-based: controls should be proportionate, staged, reviewable and responsive to new science rather than treating any imaginable catastrophe as sufficient.
Industry and consumer transition costs are real affected interests and should be reduced through phased implementation and substitute development rather than ignored.
The global nature of ozone depletion creates reciprocity/non-extraction concerns because individual producers/users can export atmospheric risk to people who do not share the benefits.
Countries with lower capacity/development needs require differentiated implementation/support rather than identical burdens irrespective of capability.
A built-in adjustment/review mechanism is morally relevant because it preserves challengeability and lets policy strengthen or relax as evidence changes.
